name: Opener Story — Uncle Ben Commitment
body: With great power comes great responsibility. Use this familiar story to create a frame where the audience commits to using what they learn for good before you teach them anything. This secures ethical commitment and raises engagement.
moral: Use a familiar story to establish ethical responsibility and get audience commitment before teaching.
useWhen: Opening activation story for presentations. Job: set the ethical frame, get audience commitment, and increase engagement before teaching begins.
hook: I commit to use what I learn today for good and in service of others.

name: Vehicle Story — From Tactics to Journeys
body: After seeing people fall through the cracks, went looking for better tactics — mentorship, sales, branding, conversion. Even when individual parts were good the overall journey felt choppy. Breakthrough: the problem was not needing more pieces but pieces that were not working together. Shifted from 'what tactic next?' to 'how does every step support the next one?'
moral: The answer is not more tactics. The answer is synced steps that support each other.
useWhen: Use to introduce the three core frameworks. Job: show the realization that disconnected tactics are not the answer — coordinated movement is.
hook: How do I make every step support the next one?
punchline: I stopped trying to stack random tactics. I started building journeys.

name: The Bitcoin Time Traveller
body:
Imagine I gave you a time machine right now — just for ten minutes. And I sent you back to 2010, where you could find your past self.

What would you tell them?

Because Bitcoin in 2010 was about eight cents. Eight cents. Today it's worth tens of thousands of dollars per coin.

So if you could go back, sit your past self down, and say: 'mate, take everything you've got. Every dollar. Every bit of savings. Put it into this weird internet money called Bitcoin. Don't ask why. Just do it.'

What do you reckon your past self would say?

They'd probably go — 'nah, that sounds risky. I don't really get it. I'll think about it. Maybe next year when I've got a bit more.'

And you'd want to shake them, right? Because YOU can see what they can't. You can see what was on the other side of that decision. The house they could've bought. The freedom they could've had. The life they could've built.

But here's the thing — the past version of you wasn't being stupid. They were just making the decision with the information they had. They couldn't see what you can see now. That's the only difference.

So — if a future version of you, ten years from now, could come back to this conversation right now… what do you reckon they'd be telling you to do?
moral:
**Moral:** Future-you, with hindsight, would always tell present-you to act on opportunity. Hesitation only LOOKS rational from inside the moment. From outside, it looks like the same mistake your past self has already made before.

**Belief installed:** The information available now is sufficient to act. Waiting for more information is just hesitation wearing a smarter outfit.
useWhen:
**Phase:** Solution awareness phase / pre-pitch / setting up the close. Mid-call.

**Use when prospect:**
- Can articulate the opportunity but isn't acting on it.
- Says 'I want to think about it' on something time-sensitive.
- Treats a window-of-opportunity decision like a routine one.

**Why this is BOTH a story AND an analogy:** Living in the Story Bank means it's reusable as a webinar / video ad / DM beat. Living in 🎨 Analogies (companion record exists) means it's deployed as a live-call reframe. Same content, two delivery contexts.
hook: If I gave you a time machine right now — just for ten minutes — and I sent you back to 2010… what would you tell them?
punchline: If a future version of you could come back to this conversation right now — what do you reckon they'd be telling you to do?

name: Do-or-Die Phone Call to Dad
body:
I was in exactly the same position as you.

I needed help in saving my business and the program was 15K. It was a stretch — but it was do-or-die. So I rang up my dad and asked him what I should do.

And he said: 'What would you do if you knew you couldn't fail?'

So I did it. And that's why I'm in this chair today.

You see — the thing is, it boils down to two things:

One, we make decisions from a place of 'what if I fail and that means we stay stuck?'

Or two, we make decisions from a place where we ask ourselves 'what if we succeed?' — and we try, and for the most part we get the result.

Some decisions have very little impact on our lives. Others will directly contribute to our success.

So — what action do you feel you need to take so that when you go to bed tonight, you have done everything you can to make XYZ a reality?
moral:
**Moral:** When the stakes are high enough, the only useful question is 'what would I do if I knew I couldn't fail?' — and the only useful answer is the action you take that night.

**Belief installed:** Self-belief comes AFTER the decision, not before. You don't wait until you're certain to act — you act and certainty follows.
useWhen:
**Phase:** Mid-to-late objection handling, especially when the prospect's hesitation is rooted in self-doubt rather than logistics. Pairs with the Self-Belief reframe (Reframe 5 in the Little Book).

**Use when prospect says:**
- "I don't know if I can do this."
- "I'm not sure if it'll work for me."
- "What if I fail?"
- "I'm scared."

**Why a story instead of an analogy:** Self-doubt isn't a logic problem — it's an identity problem. Analogies reframe thinking; stories reframe feeling. This story makes the prospect FEEL what it's like to bet on themselves and win.
hook: I needed help saving my business and the program was 15K. It was a stretch — but it was do-or-die.
punchline: What would you do if you knew you couldn't fail?

name: Origin Story — Split Homes to Belonging
body: Parents divorced at age 2, moved between homes every other week, two different lives with split values and rhythm, felt something was missing — love, connection, stability. Found nightlife years later and discovered belonging and shared energy. (Clients write their own origin using these beats.)
moral: Community mattered because belonging was missing early — not because marketing made it trendy.
useWhen: Short emotional root story. Use after About Me, before the bridge story.
hook: Before I ever knew how to build community, I knew what it felt like to miss it.
punchline: That opened the next chapter of my life.

name: Internal Story — ClickFunnels and the Clear Path
body: Signed up for ClickFunnels, six months passed without launching, realized the problem was not ability but absence of a clear path, followed a process, launched, made first $1,500 then $5,000 week.
moral: People often need a clearer path, not more confidence.
useWhen: Use during Secret #2 or internal false belief section. Job: prove that lack of clarity — not lack of capability — is the real blocker.
hook: I do not need more confidence first. I need a clearer path first.
punchline: I needed a formula I could follow.

name: External Story — Red Ocean to Deeper Connection
body: Looked around and saw a red ocean — bigger audiences, teams, budgets — realized winning is not about being louder but connecting deeper, stopped trying to dominate attention and started focusing on trust, relevance, and journey.
moral: You do not need the biggest audience. You need deeper connection and better sequencing.
useWhen: Use during Secret #3 or external false belief section. Job: show that circumstances influence the game but do not dictate the result.
hook: My current situation is not the thing that gets the final say.
punchline: Those things influence the game. They do not get to dictate the result.

name: Bridge Story — The Broken Journey
body: Noticed business owners losing not because of weak offers but broken journeys — post, comment, DM, link, register, reminder, event — people kept falling through the cracks. Most people do not have a traffic problem. They have a disconnected journey problem.
moral: The real issue is not always the offer or effort. It is the disconnect between steps.
useWhen: Use immediately after the origin story. Job: pivot away from founder narrative and into the market problem.
hook: The sale is often lost before the pitch.
punchline: So I went looking for the real answer.

name: The Pilot and the Plane Ticket
body:
It's completely normal that the other side doesn't make sense. It's completely normal that you're having a disconnect seeing yourself at that destination. It's not your job to know exactly how you're gonna get there.

When you buy a plane ticket, you don't go to the pilot and say: 'Hey pilot, let me take a look around your cockpit because I want to make sure that you know how to get me from London to New York.'

That's not your responsibility.

It's the pilot's responsibility to get you from London to New York. Your only responsibility is to show up on your flight.

Show up on your flight. Strap on your seat belt. And let's go for this ride.

As long as you can do that — as long as you can buy your ticket and show up — we'll do the rest. We'll bring you to your destination.

But you gotta show up. You gotta buy the ticket. You gotta hop on the flight, and you have to come along for the ride.

Are you willing to do that?
moral:
**Moral:** Trying to do BOTH the buyer's job AND the pilot's job is what's keeping the prospect stuck on the runway. Once they trust the pilot, they free up all the energy that was being spent on figuring out the route.

**Belief installed:** You don't need to understand HOW to start. You need to commit to SHOWING UP, and the system handles the rest.
useWhen:
**Phase:** Late objection handling. Used when prospect understands the offer logically but can't see themselves on the other side, OR when they want to micromanage HOW the result happens before committing.

**Use when prospect says:**
- "I can't see how this will work for me."
- "How exactly does this work? Walk me through every step."
- "I'm a do-it-yourself kind of person."
- "I need to understand the whole roadmap before I commit."
hook: When you buy a plane ticket, you don't go to the pilot and ask to inspect the cockpit.
punchline: Show up on your flight. Strap on your seat belt. And let's go for this ride.
